passages.happening:
Some men come down from Judea to the church at Antioch and teach the believers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (verse 1). Paul and Barnabas argue hard against them. So the church sends Paul, Barnabas and some others up to Jerusalem, to put the question to the apostles and elders (verse 2).

On the way, as they pass through Phoenicia and Samaria, they tell how Gentiles have turned to God, and the news brings “great joy to all the brothers” (verse 3). In Jerusalem the church, the apostles and the elders welcome them, and they report all that God has done (verse 4).

Then some believers from the party of the Pharisees stand up and say, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Circumcision is the cutting away of the foreskin, the loose fold of skin at the tip of the penis. For Jews it was the sign of God's covenant, his binding promise, made with Abraham, and it was done to baby boys on their eighth day. A Gentile (anyone who is not a Jew) who fully joined the Jewish people was circumcised too. Such a convert was called a proselyte.

Who were the men who said the Gentile believers must be circumcised? Luke says they were ‘believers from the party of the Pharisees’. The Pharisees were a Jewish group known for keeping the law of Moses with great care. These men believed in Jesus. They were not enemies of the church. They were members of it.

Their case deserves to be heard in its strongest form, the way they would have put it. God himself gave circumcision to Abraham, and he called it everlasting. The Law said that a foreigner who wanted to share Israel's Passover must first be circumcised. Jesus is the Messiah of Israel, the promised King of the Jews. So anyone who wants to belong to Israel's Messiah should join Israel in the way God's own Law had always laid down: by circumcision, and by keeping the commandments. Their Bible said nothing about God one day setting this aside. To them, welcoming Gentiles without it looked like treating God's word as if it did not matter. They were Bible-believing men, and they were taking the Bible seriously.

But the men who came to Antioch went further than saying circumcision was good. They said, ‘you cannot be saved’ without it. That is why Paul and Barnabas fight so hard. The question is no longer about a custom. It is about what saves a person.

Notice how the church handles a question that could split it in two. It does not form two churches. It sends people to talk it through with the apostles and the elders in Jerusalem. And on the way, the news of Gentiles turning to God brings ‘great joy’ to the believers in Samaria, the very people most Jews had long kept apart from (chapter 8).
passages.ot:
The men who wanted Gentiles circumcised had the Scriptures on their side, and they knew it. God told Abraham, “This is My covenant with you and your descendants after you, which you are to keep: Every male among you must be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10). He added, “My covenant in your flesh will be an everlasting covenant” (Genesis 17:13).

The Passover law said the same of outsiders: “If a foreigner resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised” (Exodus 12:48). Even Isaiah, who foresaw foreigners joining the LORD and worshipping in his house, speaks of them as people “who hold fast to My covenant” (Isaiah 56:6).

But the Law also spoke of a deeper circumcision: “Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more” (Deuteronomy 10:16). Both sides at the coming meeting knew these words.
passages.asks: The men from Judea loved God's law and wanted to honour it, and they were still wrong about what saves. Ask what you add to Jesus, without saying so aloud, before you will count someone a real Christian: a style of worship, a political side, a way of dressing, a list of rules. And notice how the first church faced a question that could have torn it apart. It met, it listened, and it went to the Scriptures together.

passages.t: Peter: ‘saved through grace, just as they are’
passages.happening:
The apostles and elders meet to look into the matter (verse 6). After much discussion Peter stands up. He reminds them that God chose him, years before, to bring the good news to Gentiles, and they believed (verse 7). “And God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us” (verse 8). “He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith” (verse 9).

“Now then, why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?” (verse 10). “On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Peter is speaking of Cornelius, the Roman officer in chapter 10. While Peter was still preaching in his house, the Holy Spirit fell on the Gentiles who were listening, and the Jewish believers with Peter were amazed (10:44-45). Peter's argument rests on what God did. God gave these Gentiles the same Spirit he gave the apostles at Pentecost, before anyone circumcised them. Who could now say they did not belong?

‘He cleansed their hearts by faith.’ Jewish law spoke a great deal of clean and unclean. Gentiles were thought of as unclean. Peter says God has already made their hearts clean, and he did it through faith, not through circumcision.

A yoke was a wooden frame laid across the necks of oxen so that they could pull a load. Peter is not mocking the law. Many Jews loved it, and the Psalms sing of delight in it. His point is that no one, not even the best of Israel, kept it well enough to be saved by keeping it. So it makes no sense to put on new believers a load that the old believers never carried well.

Then comes a surprising turn. Peter does not say, ‘they are saved just as we are’. He says ‘we are saved, just as they are’. The Gentiles are not the exception, let in by a side door. They show the way everyone has always been saved: by the grace of the Lord Jesus.

These are Peter's last words in Acts. From here on the story follows Paul.
passages.ot:
Peter's words about clean hearts and the Spirit echo the prophets. God promised through Ezekiel, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26), and “I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27). Jeremiah called the men of Judah to “remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4). The deepest circumcision was always the heart's.

And the law Peter calls a heavy yoke was also loved: “Oh, how I love Your law! All day long it is my meditation” (Psalm 119:97). Both things are true. The law was good, and no one was saved by keeping it perfectly.
passages.hard:
How does this meeting fit with what Paul writes in Galatians 2? There Paul says he went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, “in response to a revelation” (Galatians 2:2), and met the leaders privately. He says, “not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek” (Galatians 2:3), and that James, Peter and John gave him and Barnabas “the right hand of fellowship” (Galatians 2:9).

Readers answer in three ways, as the book page sets out. Many think Galatians 2 tells this same council from Paul's side: the same people, the same question, the same result. Others think it is the earlier famine visit of Acts 11, because Paul went after a revelation and the leaders asked him to ‘remember the poor’ (Galatians 2:10); on that view Galatians was written before this council, which would explain why Paul never mentions its letter. A third view sees Galatians 2 as a private meeting of its own.

Galatians also tells of a sharp quarrel at Antioch. Peter used to eat with Gentile believers, but when ‘certain men came from James’, he drew back, and Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11-14). Depending on the view taken, that quarrel came before this council or after it. These notes set out the views and do not settle them. On every view, Peter, James and Paul came to agree on the main thing: Gentiles do not have to be circumcised to belong to Christ.
passages.asks: Peter says, ‘we are saved, just as they are’, not the other way round. Ask whether you quietly think of yourself as the insider, the one God accepts more easily than the newcomer. And ask what loads you lay on newer believers that you have never carried well yourself.

passages.t: James: ‘The words of the prophets agree’
passages.happening:
The whole assembly falls silent as Barnabas and Paul tell of the signs and wonders God has done among the Gentiles through them (verse 12).

Then James speaks: “Brothers, listen to me!” (verse 13). Simon Peter has told how God first visited the Gentiles “to take from them a people to be His own” (verse 14). The prophets agree, as it is written: “After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David” (verse 16), “so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name” (verse 17).

“It is my judgment, therefore, that we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God” (verse 19). Instead they should write to them, asking them to keep away from four things: food polluted by idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals, and blood (verse 20). “For Moses has been proclaimed in every city from ancient times and is read in the synagogues on every Sabbath” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Barnabas and Paul do not argue. They tell what God has done. ‘Signs and wonders’ is the language used of Moses in Egypt. God is at work among the Gentiles as he once worked for Israel.

This James is not the apostle James, the brother of John, who was killed in chapter 12. He is James the brother of Jesus (Galatians 1:19; Mark 6:3), who did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5) but became the leader of the church in Jerusalem. He was known for his faithfulness to the law, which is why his voice carries such weight with the believers from among the Pharisees. The Jewish historian Josephus reports that he was stoned in Jerusalem about AD 62.

He calls Peter ‘Simon’, the old Hebrew form of his name. And he says God has taken from the Gentiles ‘a people to be His own’. That phrase was used of Israel. Now it is used of Gentiles, who are joined to God's people as Gentiles.

Then James turns to the prophet Amos. The ‘fallen tent of David’ is the royal house of David, fallen into ruin. James sees it rebuilt in Jesus, the Son of David, and the nations coming in. His quotation follows the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, which reads that the rest of humanity ‘may seek the Lord’. The Hebrew text, which most English Bibles translate in Amos, reads that Israel will ‘possess the remnant of Edom’. In Hebrew letters ‘Edom’ and ‘adam’ (meaning ‘mankind’) look very alike, and some think that lies behind the difference. Both forms say that nations who bear God's name belong in David's restored kingdom.

Verse 21 is read in more than one way. Some take it to mean: since Moses is read in every town, these four things will help Gentile believers live at peace with their Jewish neighbours, who care deeply about them. Others take it to mean: Moses already has many teachers, so there is no need to press his whole law on the Gentiles.
passages.ot:
James quotes Amos. In the Hebrew text, as most English Bibles have it, God says, “In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David” (Amos 9:11), “that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name” (Amos 9:12).

Other prophets saw the same day. Zechariah wrote, “On that day many nations will join themselves to the LORD, and they will become My people” (Zechariah 2:11). The phrase ‘a people to be His own’ echoes what Moses said to Israel: “The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth” (Deuteronomy 7:6).
passages.hard:
What were the four requirements for (verse 20), and do they still bind Christians? Readers understand them in several ways.

Many see them as drawn from Leviticus 17 and 18. Those chapters laid certain rules not only on Israel but also on ‘the foreigner living among them’: no sacrifices to other gods, no eating of blood, the blood of a hunted animal drained out, and no forbidden sexual unions. On this reading the four requirements are what the Law itself had asked of Gentiles living among God's people, so that Gentile and Jewish believers could share one table and one church. Others note that the match is loose and that Luke does not name Leviticus.

Others point out that each of the four was tied to pagan temple worship, where meat offered to idols, blood and sexual rites often went together. On this reading the requirements mean: make a clean break with the temples.

The copies of Acts also differ here. Codex Bezae, a Greek and Latin manuscript of the fifth century, and some other copies leave out ‘strangled’ and add a form of the golden rule, put negatively: do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself. That turns the list into rules about conduct alone. Most textual scholars think these changes came later.

Do the rules still bind? Most churches have not treated the food rules as a law for all time. They note that Paul, who carried this decision to the churches (16:4), later told the Corinthians that food “does not bring us closer to God” (1 Corinthians 8:8) and that meat sold in the market could be eaten unless eating it would wound someone's conscience (1 Corinthians 10:25-28). Some Christians hold that the requirements still apply, because the Law gave them to Gentiles living among God's people. All agree that the call to keep away from sexual immorality stands, since the New Testament repeats it often. This is a question on which faithful Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: James listened to the stories, then went to the Scriptures, and then gave a judgment that asked something of both sides: the Jewish believers gave up circumcision for Gentiles, and the Gentile believers gave up things that would hurt their Jewish brothers. Ask what your freedom might cost someone else at your table. And ask whether, when Christians disagree, you begin with what God has done and what the Scriptures say.

passages.t: The letter: ‘It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us’
passages.happening:
The apostles and elders, with the whole church, decide to send two leaders to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas (verse 22). They carry a letter from ‘the apostles and the elders, your brothers’ to the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia (verse 23).

Some men went out from us without our authorization, the letter says, and unsettled you (verse 24). So we are sending chosen men with “our beloved Barnabas and Paul” (verse 25), men who have risked their lives for the name of the Lord Jesus (verse 26). Judas and Silas will tell you the same things in person (verse 27).

“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements” (verse 28): keep away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. “You will do well to avoid these things. Farewell” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The letter is written in the ordinary form of a Greek letter of the time, with a greeting at the start and ‘Farewell’ at the end. It is short and warm. It calls the Gentile believers ‘brothers’. It says plainly that the men who troubled Antioch did not speak for Jerusalem. And it sends two trusted men to say it in person, so that no one can twist its words. One of them, Silas, will soon become Paul's partner.

‘It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.’ The church does not claim a voice from heaven. It listened to what God had done, weighed it by the Scriptures, argued it out, and came to one mind, and it believed the Spirit had led it there.

Churches have looked back to this meeting when they think about how the church decides. Catholic Christians hold that a council of bishops together with the pope can define the faith without error. Orthodox Christians honour seven great councils, from Nicaea in 325 to the second council of Nicaea in 787, as the voice of the whole church guided by the Spirit. Many Protestant churches hold that councils are a real help but can be wrong; the Westminster Confession (chapter 31) says that all councils since the apostles ‘may err, and many have erred’, so Scripture stands above them. Congregational churches, such as Baptists, hold that each local church governs itself under Christ, and that wider gatherings advise rather than command. These notes do not choose between them.

Notice what the letter settles and what it does not. It is written to Gentile believers. It tells them they need not be circumcised or take on the whole law of Moses. It says nothing to Jewish believers about giving up circumcision or the law, and it does not call the law bad. Later in Acts, the Jewish believers in Jerusalem are still ‘zealous for the law’ (21:20), and Paul himself wrote, “Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised” (1 Corinthians 7:18). Jewish believers who kept the law were honouring the God who gave it. The council made room for Gentiles without asking Jews to stop being Jews.
passages.ot:
The four requirements echo the rules the Law laid on the foreigner living among Israel: “If anyone from the house of Israel or a foreigner living among them eats any blood, I will set My face against that person” (Leviticus 17:10), and the laws on sexual sin close with, “you must not commit any of these abominations”, a command laid on the native-born and the foreigner alike (Leviticus 18:26). The ban on blood is older still. God told Noah, the father of all nations after the flood, “But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4).

Bringing a hard question to the leaders also had roots in the Law. Moses told Israel's judges, “bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it” (Deuteronomy 1:17).
passages.asks: The church settled its hardest question by listening, by searching the Scriptures, by speaking honestly, and by sending people to explain in person. Ask how you handle a disagreement in your church: by rumour and sides, or by meeting face to face. And notice that the letter set Gentiles free without asking Jews to give up their way of life. Ask whether you can make room for believers whose practice differs from yours without looking down on them.

passages.happening:
The men are sent off and go down to Antioch. There they gather the church and deliver the letter (verse 30). “When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message” (verse 31).

Judas and Silas, who are prophets, say much to encourage and strengthen the believers (verse 32). After some time they are sent back in peace to those who sent them (verse 33). Paul and Barnabas stay on in Antioch, with many others, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Think how this letter sounded in Antioch. Gentile believers had been told by visitors from Judea that they were not saved. Now the leaders in Jerusalem write that they belong, without circumcision, and they call them brothers. No wonder they rejoice.

Judas and Silas are ‘prophets’. In the New Testament a prophet was not only someone who foretold the future. A prophet spoke God's word to strengthen and comfort people. Paul later wrote that one who prophesies “speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort” (1 Corinthians 14:3). That is what these two do.

Your Bible may jump from verse 33 to verse 35. Some later copies of Acts add a verse 34, saying that Silas decided to stay in Antioch. The oldest copies do not have it, so most modern Bibles, the Berean Standard Bible among them, leave the number empty or put the words in a footnote. Many scholars think a copyist added it to explain why Silas is back in Antioch in verse 40.
passages.ot:
The joy at Antioch is the joy of good news from far away, as Proverbs says: “Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25:25). Isaiah sang of the same thing: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace” (Isaiah 52:7).

The prophets of Israel also spoke God's word to strengthen his people in hard days, as when Haggai told the builders of the temple, “I am with you” (Haggai 1:13).
passages.asks: A letter that told people they truly belonged brought a whole church to joy. Ask whom you could encourage this week with a word, a visit or a letter. And ask whether the way you speak about the faith leaves people burdened, or strengthened.

passages.t: A sharp disagreement: Paul, Barnabas and Mark
passages.happening:
Some time later Paul says to Barnabas, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing” (verse 36).

Barnabas wants to take John, also called Mark (verse 37). But Paul thinks it best not to, “because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work” (verse 38). “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company” (verse 39). Barnabas takes Mark and sails for Cyprus. Paul chooses Silas and sets out, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord (verse 40), and travels through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
Luke tells this plainly, and it is worth reading slowly. These are two good men. Barnabas, whose name means ‘Son of Encouragement’ (4:36), once stood up for Saul when the whole church in Jerusalem was afraid of him (9:27). Paul has just risked his life with him across Cyprus and Galatia. They have stood side by side before the council. And now they cannot agree.

Each had a reason. Mark had left them in Pamphylia on the first trip (13:13), and Paul thinks the work ahead is too hard to take a man who might turn back again. Barnabas sees a young man worth a second chance, and Mark was his cousin (Colossians 4:10). Luke does not say who was right. He simply says the disagreement was ‘so sharp’. The Greek word is the one from which English gets ‘paroxysm’, a sudden fit of strong feeling.

They part, and the work does not stop. Now there are two teams instead of one: Barnabas and Mark to Cyprus, Paul and Silas to the churches of Syria, Cilicia and Galatia. This is the last time Barnabas appears in Acts.

And the story of Mark does not end here. Years later, Mark is with Paul again, named among his ‘fellow workers’ (Philemon 24), and Paul tells the church at Colossae to welcome him if he comes. Near the end of his life Paul writes, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). The young man Paul would not take became a man Paul asked for. The early church also remembered a Mark as the writer of the second Gospel; the book page for Mark sets out what that tradition rests on.
passages.ot:
The Scriptures do not hide quarrels between good people. When Abram and Lot's herdsmen fought, Abram said, “Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are brothers” (Genesis 13:8), and the two went separate ways in peace.

The Psalms hold up the better way: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1). Paul and Barnabas fell short of it for a time, and God still kept his work going.
passages.asks: Two faithful men quarrelled so sharply that they parted, and Luke does not hide it. Ask whether you expect too much of Christian leaders, or too little of God, who kept working through both of them. If a friendship in your church has broken, ask whether, like Paul and Mark, there might one day be a road back. And if you were once the one who turned back, remember Mark. Your story is not over.
